4.1 The question and the endogeneity
What are institutions?
Douglass North (1990): “the humanly devised constraints that structure political, economic,
and social interaction” — formal rules (laws, constitutions, regulation) and informal ones
(norms, conventions). They set the incentives and transaction costs that shape economic
performance. Political institutions distribute power; economic institutions (property rights,
contract enforcement, entry barriers) follow from them and shape incentives to invest and
innovate:
political institutions → economic institutions → incentives → investment, innovation, growth .
AJR contrast inclusive institutions, which protect broad property rights, with extractive ones,
which transfer resources to a narrow elite.
Three explanations compete for why some countries are rich: geography (climate, disease, endow-
ments), culture (values, trust), and institutions.
Why are some countries rich and others poor? Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (AJR, 2001)
argue that institutions — secure property rights, constraints on elites — are the fundamental cause.
Across countries, log GDP per capita in 1995 rises strongly with protection against expropriation
risk (1985–95 average). But the correlation has four readings: institutions raise income; income
buys better institutions (reverse causality); both; or a third factor drives both (omitted variable).
OLS cannot distinguish them.

Where early European settlers faced high death rates from malaria and yellow fever (West Africa, much of South and South-East Asia), they did not settle; colonizers set up extractive institutions designed to transfer resources. Where mortality was low (Australia, New Zealand, North America), they settled and built inclusive institutions that protected property — their own. Figure 5: Left, first stage: protection against expropriation against log settler mortality. Right, reduced
form: log GDP per capita against log settler mortality. The IV estimate is the ratio of the two slopes.
Source: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2001).
Reading the figures. The left panel is the first stage: Australia, New Zealand, the United States
and Canada sit top-left (low mortality, strong institutions), Mali and Nigeria bottom-right. The
right panel is the reduced form, with the same ordering in income. Neither panel alone is the causal
effect of institutions; their ratio is. Note that the first figure alone cannot be read causally — it is
the correlation the whole exercise is designed to decompose.
4.3 Is the exclusion restriction credible?
The instrument is relevant; the debate is about exclusion. Settler mortality reflects the disease
environment, and disease may affect income today directly — through health and productivity
— not only through institutions. AJR respond by controlling for current malaria, latitude and
continent dummies. Others question the mortality data themselves (Albouy 2012): with revised
data the first stage weakens. The case shows that a strong first stage does not settle validity:
relevance is a statistical question, exclusion an economic one.
Why persistence? Colonial-era elites kept de facto power after independence; legal origins shaped
property rights and regulation; inclusive institutions encouraged education and innovation, while
extractive ones entrenched inequality and blocked entry. The policy lesson AJR draw is that reform
must address political constraints, not only technocratic fixes, and that institutional change is slow
and path dependent.
Discussion. How credible is the exclusion restriction? Can institutional persistence also explain
income differences within countries? Do cases such as North and South Korea — one people, one
geography, two sets of institutions — or Botswana fit the framework?
Why IV is above OLS here. Measurement error again: “expropriation risk” is a noisy proxy for
institutions, which attenuates OLS. Reverse causality alone would bias OLS upward , so attenuation
must dominate.
